results.title: Full article: Artificial intelligence (AI) and ethical concerns
results.content: This research aims to understand the predominant ethical concerns associated with AI systems and technology usage across diverse domains discussed in past studies. *Ethics and Information Technology* has published the most research (forty-four) on AI and ethics, with 1561 citations. Artificial intelligence (AI) systems have become an integral part of our daily lives, and this widespread breakthrough of these technologies in every sphere underscores the urgency and need to examine and address the ethical issues associated with the fair usage of these innovative and intelligent technologies (Munoko et al., Citation2020). Additionally, discussions on regulatory initiatives and the ethical implications of AI systems have increased public awareness, leading to the implementation of proper, stringent measures to safeguard data and deter unauthorized or inappropriate use, including anonymization and data encryption (Larson et al., Citation2020). Through its thorough bibliometric and thematic analysis, this research helps understand the ethical dilemmas concerning AI systems through diverse theoretical dimensions, providing a more holistic view of the field.

results.title: AI and cross-cultural convergence in academic writing quality
results.content: Despite these concerns, AI tools continue to offer meaningful benefits, especially to non-native English speakers, by improving writing quality and expanding access to academic discourse (Alharbi, 2023 AI in the foreign language classroom: a pedagogical overview of automated writing assistance tools. The global implications of English-language dominance and the growing integration of AI tools in academic writing have garnered increasing scholarly attention. How has the academic writing quality of social sciences abstracts evolved from 2012 to 2024, and how does it vary between native and non-native English-speaking countries, and across gender, regional and income-based classifications? While the abstracts served as the primary material for evaluating academic writing quality, measured through established readability metrics, the accompanying metadata enabled analysis of variations in writing complexity and potential AI influence across dimensions such as author gender, geographic origin, funding status and other publication characteristics. This section interprets the study’s findings in relation to existing debates on writing quality, digital access and AI-driven language support in academic publishing.
